title: Emergencies intensify gendered precarity in cultural work while women’s cultural labor sustains heritage, community resilience and recovery
source_unit: UNESCO, Voices of Courage: A Global Survey on Women, Culture and Emergencies
geography: More than 120 countries; women artists, cultural professionals and heritage professionals

observations.period: 2026 publication; experiences of 1,470 women across emergency contexts

denominator.unit: survey respondents from more than 120 countries

insufficient_funding_market_access.unit: per cent reporting insufficient funding and market access

creative_work_disruption.unit: per cent reporting disruption to cultural and creative work

economic_instability_livelihood_loss.unit: per cent reporting economic instability and loss of livelihood

trauma_burnout.unit: per cent experiencing trauma and burnout

observations.method: UNESCO global survey with personal testimonies and case studies examining women’s experiences before, during and after emergencies across culture and heritage work.
observations.uncertainty: The survey page does not provide the full sampling frame, response rate, country-by-country weighting or denominator for every subgroup; reported prevalence should not be read as a representative estimate of all women cultural workers globally.
observations.subgroup: Women artists, cultural professionals and heritage professionals exposed to armed conflict, civil unrest, natural hazards and health crises.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported precarity may reflect concentration of the survey among affected or connected networks; emergency exposure and sectoral instability may vary substantially by occupation, country and crisis type.

observations.period: 2026 publication; displacement, continuity and access to support during emergencies

denominator.unit: survey respondents from more than 120 countries

emergency_displacement.unit: per cent forced to leave their homes because of an emergency

continued_cultural_work.unit: per cent able to continue cultural and creative work fully or significantly during crises

support_access.unit: approximately 2 in 5 women accessing any form of support during emergencies

institutional_recognition.unit: per cent of public institutions and civil society organizations recognizing that emergencies significantly exacerbate gender inequalities

observations.method: Survey measures of displacement, continuity of creative work, emergency support and institutional recognition, supplemented by testimonies and cases.
observations.uncertainty: Support access is not disaggregated here by type, adequacy, timing or local availability; continued work does not mean safe, fairly paid or sustainable work.
observations.subgroup: Women cultural and heritage workers navigating emergency displacement, disrupted spaces, livelihood loss and support systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some cultural continuity may be informal, home-based or digitally mediated and therefore undercounted; institutional recognition is a perception or reported assessment rather than a complete audit of emergency plans.

observations.period: 2026 publication; gendered mechanisms linking emergency exposure to cultural work and community recovery

denominator.unit: survey respondents from more than 120 countries, with testimonies and case studies

gendered_barriers.value: Emergencies increase unpaid caregiving, restrictions on freedom of expression including artistic freedom, and gender-based violence alongside resource, protection and decision-making barriers.

cultural_resilience_role.value: Women artists and cultural and heritage professionals safeguard heritage and traditions, sustain cultural expressions, organize solidarity and contribute to recovery and peacebuilding.

recognition_gap.value: Women-led initiatives and networks are described as essential to resilience, while their contributions remain insufficiently recognized in preparedness, response and recovery mechanisms.

observations.method: Global survey synthesis combined with personal testimony, case studies and UNESCO analysis of the emergency-management cycle from preparedness through recovery.
observations.uncertainty: The report documents mechanisms and contributions but does not estimate causal effects of women-led cultural action on peace, recovery or resilience outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Women-led cultural initiatives, artists, heritage professionals, cultural networks, communities and emergency-management institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Culture can support solidarity and recovery without substituting for shelter, safety, income, health or legal protection; framing women as resilient must not shift responsibility away from institutions.

observations.period: 2026 publication; proposed gender-responsive culture-and-emergency policy response

denominator.unit: UNESCO report recommendations and Heritage Emergency Fund implementation context

recommended_support.value: The report calls for financial, psychosocial and legal support, women’s participation in decision-making, protection of rights and safety, artistic freedom and the ability to continue cultural work through the emergency cycle.

heritage_emergency_fund_reach.unit: more than 100 countries equipped through UNESCO Heritage Emergency Fund capacities and means

professionals_trained.unit: more than 4,400 professionals trained in emergency preparedness and response; nearly half women

gender_responsive_design.value: The Heritage Emergency Fund integrates gender-specific needs and meaningful participation of women and women’s organizations throughout the emergency cycle.

observations.method: UNESCO recommendations and description of Heritage Emergency Fund implementation, not an independent impact evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: Program reach and training counts do not establish adequacy, safety, local control, durable livelihood recovery or cultural outcomes for recipients.
observations.subgroup: Women artists and cultural and heritage professionals, women’s organizations, cultural institutions, emergency responders and communities affected by crises.
observations.counterinterpretation: Gender-responsive design can remain procedural if women lack decision power, flexible funding, protection and remedy; training alone cannot offset destroyed infrastructure or displacement.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO publication record for Voices of Courage, the global survey on women, culture and emergencies.
UNESCO culture-in-emergencies context and policy field.

boundary: This record adds a gendered cultural-emergency layer: crisis exposure moves through safety, displacement, unpaid care, funding, market access, artistic freedom and institutional recognition, while women’s cultural work helps sustain heritage, solidarity and recovery. It is a UNESCO global survey page with testimonies and case studies, not a fully documented probability sample, administrative crisis census, causal resilience evaluation or proof that cultural work replaces material protection.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official UNESCO Voices of Courage publication page was reviewed for publication date, sample scope, prevalence findings, emergency mechanisms, women’s resilience contributions, recommendations and Heritage Emergency Fund context; the UNESCO publication record was also checked.
